Block rules order villages arbitrarily within a block (CSI/dept), so only block boundaries are interpretable: the curve is the linear interpolation between boundary knots, and those knots are the points drawn on the two block-rule curves.

Under `r ref_display`, `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_rd_negative)`% of villages have predicted harm ($\widehat{RD}_i < 0$), causing the cumulative curve to not be monotonic. It climbs above 100% of the universal-treatment total and then falls back to 100% at full coverage, because adding the last units (predicted harm) subtracts. The excess above 100% is the predicted cost of treating the villages the model expects no benefit in.

```{r targeting curves heatmap}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8

# Heat map rather than a table. What matters in these 25 numbers is the
# gradient down each column - how much a coarser rule gives up at fixed
# coverage - and a grid of digits makes the reader reconstruct that by eye.
# rev() on the levels because ggplot draws the first factor level at the
# bottom, and the envelope belongs at the top.
#
# ONE model only, not a facet: three of these side by side is 75 numbers, and
# the cross-model comparison is what the faceted curve figure above is for. The
# reference specification is named in the title so the panel cannot be read as
# a pooled result.
#
# 100% coverage is deliberately not a column: every rule averts exactly the
# universal-treatment total there, so it would read 100.0 five times. That
# total is the policy anchor all the same, so it is carried in the subtitle and
# each cell shows the absolute deaths averted underneath its percentage.
curve_grid <- curves %>%
  dplyr::filter(model == ref_key,
                x %in% purrr::map_dbl(coverage_marks, nearest_x)) %>%
  dplyr::select(rule, x, prop_averted, deaths_averted) %>%
  mutate(
    pct      = 100 * prop_averted,
    coverage = factor(scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1),
                      levels = scales::percent(sort(coverage_marks), accuracy = 1)),
    rule     = factor(rule,
                      levels = rev(targeting_rules),
                      labels = rev(unname(rule_labels)))
  )

p_curve_grid <- ggplot(curve_grid, aes(x = coverage, y = rule, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Label colour flips on the light half of viridis so the numbers stay
  # legible at both ends of the scale.
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), colour = pct > 55),
            vjust = -0.1, size = 4.1, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(round(deaths_averted)), colour = pct > 55),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3.1, alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey15", `FALSE` = "white")) +
  # Title and subtitle are wrapped explicitly: ggplot truncates rather than
  # reflowing, and naming the specification is long enough to run off a
  # 10-inch panel on one line.
  labs(x = "Cumulative proportion of person-time", y = NULL,
       fill = "% of universal-treatment total",
       title = paste0("Cumulative predicted deaths averted\n",
                      ref_display, " (", ref_key, ") only"),
       subtitle = paste0("% of the universal-treatment total (",
                         scales::comma(total_averted, accuracy = 1),
                         " deaths), absolute count below it.\n",
                         "ONE specification only - the faceted curve figure\n",
                         "above carries the cross-model comparison.")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid       = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
        legend.position  = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = grid::unit(2.2, "cm"),
        plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "grey35"))

p_curve_grid

ggsave(file.path(figure_path,
                 paste0("targeting-heatmap-cumulative_", ref_model, ".png")),
       plot = p_curve_grid, bg = "white", width = 10, height = 4.8, dpi = 300)
```

```{r curve objects for prose}

rd_at_30       <- pick("rd", 0.30)
mort_g_at_30   <- pick("mort_grappe", 0.30)
mort_csi_at_30 <- pick("mort_csi", 0.30)
mort_d_at_30   <- pick("mort_dept", 0.30)

averted_at_30 <- curves$deaths_averted[curves$model == ref_key &
                                         curves$rule == "mort_grappe" &
                                         curves$x == nearest_x(0.30)]

# Any rule that happens to rank the predicted-harm units last overshoots 100%
# the same way the envelope does, so the peak is computed for every rule and
# model rather than for `rd` alone. mort_dept does overshoot in these data.
curve_peaks <- curves %>%
  group_by(model, rule) %>%
  summarise(peak    = 100 * max(prop_averted),
            peak_at = x[which.max(prop_averted)],
            .groups = "drop")

peak_of <- function(rule_name, key = ref_key) {
  curve_peaks$peak[curve_peaks$model == key & curve_peaks$rule == rule_name]
}

peak_at_of <- function(rule_name, key = ref_key) {
  curve_peaks$peak_at[curve_peaks$model == key & curve_peaks$rule == rule_name]
}

rd_peak    <- peak_of("rd")
rd_peak_at <- peak_at_of("rd")
```

The x-axis is the cumulative share of the region's child person-time, accrued as villages are added in each rule's rank order. There is no 100% column because there is nothing to compare there: at full coverage every rule averts the same `r scales::comma(total_averted, accuracy = 1)` deaths by construction.

My interpretation of the heatmap (all numbers `r ref_display`): Treating the highest-mortality villages up to 30% of the region's child person-time is predicted to avert `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_g_at_30)`% of the deaths that treating everyone would avert (`r scales::comma(averted_at_30, accuracy = 1)` deaths), against `r sprintf("%.0f", rd_at_30)`% for the treatment effect-ranked gold standard and 30% for person-time-proportional random allocation. The same 30% mortality rule applied in blocks gives `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_csi_at_30)`% at the CSI scale and `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_d_at_30)`% at the department scale, indicating that targetting at the village-level is more effective than coarser targetting.

The `rd` curve reaches its maximum of `r sprintf("%.0f", rd_peak)`% of the universal-treatment total at `r scales::percent(rd_peak_at, accuracy = 1)` coverage, then returns to 100% at full coverage by construction. That is not a recommendation to withhold treatment from those villages, and the bands make the reason explicit: at `r scales::percent(rd_peak_at, accuracy = 1)` coverage the envelope's own `r scales::percent(ci_level)` interval runs from `r sprintf("%.0f", band_at("rd", rd_peak_at, "lower"))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", band_at("rd", rd_peak_at, "upper"))`%, so the overshoot above 100% is well inside the noise.

**The bands are wide, and that is the main thing to take from the curve figure.** At 30% coverage the village-level mortality rule's point estimate of `r sprintf("%.0f", mort_g_at_30)`% carries an interval of `r sprintf("%.0f", band_at("mort_grappe", 0.30, "lower"))`–`r sprintf("%.0f", band_at("mort_grappe", 0.30, "upper"))`%, and the effect-ranked envelope's runs `r sprintf("%.0f", band_at("rd", 0.30, "lower"))`–`r sprintf("%.0f", band_at("rd", 0.30, "upper"))`%. Those intervals overlap heavily.

**But some comparisons survive the uncertainty and others do not, and the difference is not what you would guess from the bands alone.** Every rule within a replicate is computed from the same draw of the surface, so a *difference* between two rules can be much better or much worse determined than either level:

* **Targeting scale is robust.** The village rule beats the department rule in `r scales::percent(p_village_beats_dept, accuracy = 0.1)` of draws, and that difference has a *narrower* interval (`r sprintf("%.2f", width_diff_village_dept)` wide) than the village curve's own level (`r sprintf("%.2f", width_level_village)`). The shared surface uncertainty largely cancels. The village-versus-CSI comparison is weaker, holding in `r scales::percent(p_village_beats_csi, accuracy = 0.1)` of draws.
* **The headline gap is not robust.** The distance between the effect-ranked envelope and the village mortality rule has an interval `r sprintf("%.2f", width_diff_rd_village)` wide — *wider* than the village level itself. Uncertainty does not cancel in that contrast, because the envelope and the mortality rule respond differently to the same perturbation of the surface.

So "targeting at village scale beats department scale" is well supported here, while "mortality-based targeting recovers most of what effect-based targeting could" is a point estimate with a great deal of noise around it.

**Relative efficiency** We're defining it to be the efficiency of the given rule relative to the RD one: $R_r(x) = y_r(x) / y_{\text{rd}}(x)$ on the shared grid, the fraction of achievable benefit retained by a rule a programme could actually apply, at a given coverage. Bounded above by 1 by construction, and $\to 1$ as $x \to 1$. Unstable as $x \to 0$, so the grid is read from `r scales::percent(eff_floor)` of person-time upwards.

```{r efficiency curves}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5.4

envelope <- curves %>%
  dplyr::filter(rule == "rd") %>%
  dplyr::select(model, x, y_rd = prop_averted)

efficiency <- curves %>%
  dplyr::filter(rule != "rd", x >= eff_floor) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(envelope, by = c("model", "x")) %>%
  mutate(efficiency_ratio = prop_averted / y_rd)

# Sanity check: no feasible rule may beat the envelope.
stopifnot(all(efficiency$efficiency_ratio <= 1 + 1e-8, na.rm = TRUE))

eff_at <- function(rule_name, coverage, key = ref_key) {
  efficiency$efficiency_ratio[efficiency$model == key &
                                efficiency$rule == rule_name &
                                efficiency$x == nearest_x(coverage)]
}

eff_g_at_30   <- eff_at("mort_grappe", 0.30)
eff_csi_at_30 <- eff_at("mort_csi", 0.30)
eff_d_at_30   <- eff_at("mort_dept", 0.30)

eff_g_min <- min(efficiency$efficiency_ratio[efficiency$model == ref_key &
                                               efficiency$rule == "mort_grappe"],
                 na.rm = TRUE)

p_efficiency <- efficiency %>%
  dplyr::left_join(eff_ribbon, by = c("model", "rule", "x")) %>%
  mutate(rule        = factor(rule, levels = names(rule_labels)),
         model_label = as_model_label(model)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = efficiency_ratio, colour = rule, group = rule)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = rule),
              alpha = 0.15, colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rule_colours) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ model_label, nrow = 1,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 30)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  # No hard y-limits: a fixed lower bound of 0 would silently drop points from
  # a block with negative predicted deaths averted, which is not hypothetical
  # here - the last-ranked department has one.
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  # No drop = FALSE: `rd` is the denominator of this ratio, not a line on the
  # plot, and forcing its unused factor level into the scale would put an
  # "Effect (RD)" key in the legend with nothing drawn against it.
  scale_colour_manual(values = rule_colours, labels = rule_labels) +
  labs(x = "Cumulative proportion of person-time",
       y = "Relative efficiency \n(share of RD-ranked rule retained)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Efficiency of feasible rules relative to the gold standard") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.spacing   = grid::unit(1, "lines"))

p_efficiency

ggsave(file.path(figure_path, "targeting-efficiency.png"),
       plot = p_efficiency, bg = "white", width = 13, height = 5.4, dpi = 300)
```

Every feasible rule converges to the envelope at full coverage by construction, so the informative region is the left half, where the rules are actually distinguishable. The department curve's rise toward the envelope on the right is likely due to harm-cancellation (Boboye's positive ATE), and potentially not a scale at which department targeting becomes competitive.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Rank concordance

**Rank concordance.** $C$ is the AUROC of a targeting rule against the predicted-effect ranking, so every rule gets its own. Draw two villages at random, weighted by person-time; $C$ is the person-time-weighted probability that the rule ranks ahead whichever of the two has the larger predicted $\widehat{RD}$, with ties contributing 0.5.

Two rules pin the scale exactly rather than approximately: `random` puts every village in one block, so every pair is a tie and $C = 0.5$ — no ranking information. `rd` is the comparator, so $C = 1$. The feasible mortality rules fall in between and $C$ is on a 0.5-to-1 scale.

A block rule is scored on its block's position, not on where a village sits inside the block, so every pair of villages within one block counts as a tie. This is a different statistic from a concordance computed on aggregated CSI or department units, which never sees the within-block pairs at all and so reports almost no penalty for coarsening.

```{r concordance}

# conc_tab is built in the `targeting curves` chunk, because the curve figure
# annotates with these same values; formatting it there and here from one object
# is what stops the figure and the table drifting apart.
#
# AUC is per *rule*, not per aggregation scale. A scale-indexed version would
# answer a different question - do CSIs rank consistently against each other -
# and would never see the within-block pairs, so it could not be read alongside
# the efficiency ratio.
#
# CIs come from the same bootstrap replicates as the ribbons. `rd` and `random`
# have no interval because they are 1 and 0.5 by construction in every
# replicate, not because the interval was not computed - hence the explicit
# em-dash rather than a blank cell.
conc_tab %>%
  dplyr::left_join(conc_ci, by = c("model", "rule")) %>%
  mutate(
    ci    = dplyr::if_else(is.na(lower), "&mdash;",
                           sprintf("%.3f&ndash;%.3f", lower, upper)),
    Model = factor(model_display[model], levels = model_levels),
    rule  = factor(rule, levels = targeting_rules, labels = rule_labels)) %>%
  arrange(Model, rule) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model,
                Rule = rule,
                `AUC (rank agreement with RD)` = auc,
                `Degradation band` = ci) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits  = 3,
    escape  = FALSE,
    caption = paste("AUROC of each rule against the predicted-effect ranking,",
                    "under each specification. `random` = 0.5 and `rd` = 1",
                    "exactly, by construction, so neither carries an interval.",
                    "The band is the pointwise percentile range when the rule",
                    "ranks on a predictive draw and is judged against the",
                    "reference effect ordering; the point estimate is the best",
                    "case, so the band lies below it.")
  )
```

Correlations between predicted baseline mortality and predicted effect, with the same intervals attached:

```{r correlation table with ci}

corr_tab %>%
  dplyr::left_join(corr_ci, by = c("model", "level")) %>%
  mutate(
    Model = factor(model_display[model], levels = model_levels),
    Level = factor(level_display[level],
                   levels = unname(level_display[level_names])),
    `Spearman rho` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f&ndash;%.2f)", rho, rho_lower, rho_upper),
    `Pearson r`    = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f&ndash;%.2f)", r, r_lower, r_upper)) %>%
  arrange(Model, Level) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, Level, `n units` = n, `Spearman rho`, `Pearson r`) %>%
  # Posterior, not degradation: a correlation does not rank and score on the
  # same quantity, so it carries no winner's curse and the within-replicate
  # interval is the right one here.
  knitr::kable(escape = FALSE,
               caption = paste("Point estimate with 95% posterior interval",
                               "over the predictive draws."))
```

```{r concordance objects for prose}

conc_grappe <- conc_of("mort_grappe")

conc_wrong_share <- 1 - conc_grappe

# C counts every mis-ranked pair alike; the efficiency ratio weights each by the
# deaths at stake. If C sits below the efficiency ratio, the rule must be erring
# mostly on pairs where little separates the two villages. Check that directly:
# compare the mean RD gap inside correctly- and incorrectly-ranked pairs, and
# the share of all pairwise RD difference that the wrong ones carry.
pair_gap <- local({
  mu0 <- pred_table$mu0; rd <- pred_table$rd; w <- pred_table$person_time
  W <- outer(w, w); diag(W) <- 0
  higher_mort <- outer(mu0, mu0, ">")
  higher_rd   <- outer(rd, rd, ">")
  gap         <- abs(outer(rd, rd, "-"))
  right <- W * higher_mort * higher_rd
  wrong <- W * higher_mort * !higher_rd
  list(gap_right   = sum(right * gap) / sum(right),
       gap_wrong   = sum(wrong * gap) / sum(wrong),
       stake_wrong = sum(wrong * gap) / (sum(right * gap) + sum(wrong * gap)))
})
```

Under `r ref_display`, the village-level mortality rule scores `r sprintf("%.2f", conc_grappe)`. Read literally: draw two villages at random, weighted by person-time, and the rule puts them in the correct order — higher predicted benefit first — about `r scales::percent(conc_grappe, accuracy = 1)`^★^ of the time.

**How much of that is structural, specification by specification.**

```{r structural notes}
#| results: asis
#| echo: false

# One bullet per specification rather than one paragraph for a chosen model:
# whether the Matern field cancels in the arm contrast is the single largest
# determinant of these numbers, and it differs across the three rows of every
# figure above.
for (this_key in model_keys) {
  cat("* **", model_display[[this_key]], "** (`", this_key, "`, AUC = ",
      sprintf("%.3f", conc_of("mort_grappe", this_key)), "). ",
      model_struct[[this_key]], "\n", sep = "")
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Conclusions

All figures are given for three specifications; the numbers quoted here are `r ref_display` (`r ref_key`) unless stated otherwise.

**Mortality-based targeting recovers most, but not all, of what effect-based targeting could.** In relative terms the village rule retains `r sprintf("%.2f", eff_g_at_30)` of the achievable benefit at 30% coverage under perfect knowledge of the fitted surface, and `r sprintf("%.2f", eff_band_at("mort_grappe", 0.30, "lower"))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", eff_band_at("mort_grappe", 0.30, "upper"))` once the ranking has to be made from a draw of that surface rather than from the surface itself. It never drops below `r sprintf("%.2f", eff_g_min)` anywhere above `r scales::percent(eff_floor)` coverage. These are one-sided degradation bands, not symmetric confidence intervals: the point estimate is the best case and the band is what estimation error costs.

**Targeting scale matters more than the choice of ranking variable — and this is the finding that survives the uncertainty.** Applying the same mortality rule in blocks costs more than switching from effect to mortality does. At 30% coverage the village rule retains `r sprintf("%.2f", eff_g_at_30)`, CSI blocks `r sprintf("%.2f", eff_csi_at_30)` and department blocks `r sprintf("%.2f", eff_d_at_30)`. The village-over-department ordering holds in `r scales::percent(p_village_beats_dept, accuracy = 0.1)` of bootstrap draws, and the village-versus-department difference is *better* determined than either curve's level — the shared surface uncertainty cancels. If a programme can act at village level, that is where the return is.

**The rank statistic and the magnitude statistic tell a consistent story.** Village-level mortality is a fair discriminator of treatment benefit ($C$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", conc_grappe)`, falling to `r sprintf("%.2f", conc_ci$lower[conc_ci$model == ref_key & conc_ci$rule == "mort_grappe"])`–`r sprintf("%.2f", conc_ci$upper[conc_ci$model == ref_key & conc_ci$rule == "mort_grappe"])` when the ranking is made from a draw rather than from the fitted surface, in AUROC terms) yet retains far more benefit than that suggests, because the pairs it mis-ranks are pairs where there was less at stake: `r scales::percent(conc_wrong_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of pairs go the wrong way but carry `r scales::percent(pair_gap$stake_wrong, accuracy = 0.1)` of the benefit difference. Under the two single-Matérn specifications this is partly an artefact of the model forcing the ATE to be proportional to control-arm mortality; the two-Matérn row is the check on that.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Caveats

1. **How much of the agreement is structural depends on the specification, which is why three are shown.** Under both single-Matérn models the shared field cancels in the arm contrast and $\widehat{RD}_i$ is a deterministic rescaling of $\hat\mu^0_i$, so the whole targeting comparison rests on a single treatment-by-space term — modestly supported in the linear case (LRT $\chi^2$ = 8.1 on 2 df, $p$ = 0.017; $\Delta$AIC $\approx$ 4) and not supported at all in the spline case (LRT $\chi^2$ = 18.2 on 12 df, $p$ = 0.11). The two-Matérn model gives the effect its own spatial field and does not force the proportionality, so where the three rows of a figure agree the result is not an artefact of that forcing, and where they disagree the disagreement is the finding.
2. **Uncertainty is propagated, but only conditional on the fitted covariance parameters.** The curves, $C$, $\rho$ and the efficiency ratios carry `r scales::percent(ci_level)` pointwise bands from `r B_boot` predictive draws. Those on the curves and ratios are one-sided *degradation* bands — what it costs to rank on an estimate rather than on the fitted surface — not symmetric confidence intervals; the correlation intervals are posterior intervals. What they do **not** carry is uncertainty in the Matérn range and smoothness, which are held at their estimates, nor any uncertainty from the choice of specification, which the three-model presentation shows rather than quantifies. The predicted-harm villages still should not be read as evidence of harm — the trial as a whole showed benefit.

### Still deferred

- **Covariance-parameter uncertainty.** The bootstrap holds $\rho$, $\nu$ and $\lambda$ at their point estimates. Propagating them needs a refit-based scheme, which the two-Matérn model's 2.77 h fit time rules out at any useful $B$.
- **Simultaneous rather than pointwise bands.** The ribbons cover each coverage level individually, not the curve as a whole.
- **Specification uncertainty as a quantity.** Showing three specifications side by side displays the sensitivity but does not put a number on it, and no resampling scheme addresses it.

## Figure 3 hand-off

```{r save figure 3 objects}
#| include: false

# Everything the manuscript's Figure 3 (primary-model targeting curves with
# their degradation envelopes) needs, bundled into one .rda so the figure script
# never has to attach spaMM, read a ~54 MB fit, or redraw the O(n^2) concordance
# bootstrap. This document owns every expensive and stochastic step; the figure
# script downstream is pure presentation and depends only on this file.
#
# The multi-model objects are saved whole rather than pre-filtered to the primary
# specification. The figure script names `ref_key` itself and filters, exactly as
# 06B does, so which model is "primary" stays visible in the figure code rather
# than being silently baked in here - and a coauthor who wants the three-panel
# version has the other two specifications on hand without re-rendering 07.
fig3_meta <- list(
  ref_key     = ref_key,        # "gen_krig_int": the primary (linear treatment-by-space interaction) model
  ref_display = ref_display,
  model_display = model_display, # keyed display names, in case a panel is labelled
  B_boot      = B_boot,          # draws behind every band, for the caption
  ci_level    = ci_level,        # nominal band coverage, for the caption
  eff_floor   = eff_floor,       # coverage floor below which efficiency ratios are unstable
  x_grid      = x_grid)

# One object per figure ingredient. Comments name what each carries so the
# figure script - which never sees the code that built them - can be read alone.
save(
  curves_ci,    # point-estimate curves joined to the degradation ribbon: model, rule, x, prop_averted, lower, upper, median
  block_knots,  # CSI/department block-boundary knots (the dots on the two step rules)
  conc_tab,     # rank concordance (AUC) with the RD ordering, per model x rule - the panel annotation
  eff_ribbon,   # efficiency-ratio degradation band, if a second panel is wanted
  rule_labels,  # display labels for the five ranking rules
  rule_colours, # colours for the five ranking rules
  fig3_meta,
  file = here("data", "targeting_fig3_objects.rda"))
```
